summary: Defines SNMP management objects for the NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A control panel for the helper that finds shortcuts across networks without broadcast.

questions: what objects does the nhrp mib define
how do i manage nhrp with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP management objects for watching and configuring NHRP clients and servers.

tldr.problem: NHRP lets machines on a non-broadcast network find the next hop toward a destination, but operators had no standard way to inspect or configure NHRP clients and servers over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2677 defines a MIB module, nhrpMIB, with a General group (cache and purge tables), a Client group and a Server group, each made of tables for configuration, state and statistics.
tldr.outcome: Network management systems can read caches, registrations and counters from NHRP devices and create or change some of them, while security settings are deliberately left out of the MIB.

today: RFC 2677 is a Proposed Standard from August 1999, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes management objects for the protocol in RFC 2332.

sections.title: What the NHRP MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2677 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it describes managed objects for the Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP) as defined in RFC 2332.

The MIB module is named nhrpMIB and sits under mib-2 at number 71. Its last-updated stamp is August 26, 1999, and its revision history has one entry: the initial version, published as this RFC. The module is written in SMIv2. A SMIv1 version can be produced by translation, and it must be semantically equivalent except for objects omitted because they cannot be translated (those using Counter64).
sections.plainLanguage: NHRP finds shortcuts across a network. This document is the list of gauges and switches that let you look at the shortcut-finder and tune it.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
The RFC situates the MIB inside the SNMP Management Framework, which it says presently has five major components: an overall architecture (RFC 2571); the Structure of Management Information, SMIv1 and SMIv2 (SMIv2 is in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580); message protocols (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3); protocol operations for accessing management information; and a set of fundamental applications plus view-based access control.

Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, the MIB, and objects in it are defined using the SMI. The RFC stresses that SNMPv2c is not an Internet standards track protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is the common language for asking network devices questions. The MIB is the list of questions you are allowed to ask.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The NHRP MIB contains three groups: the General Group, the Client Group and the Server Group. The General Group applies to both NHRP clients and servers. The Client Group applies only to NHRP clients (NHCs) and the Server Group only to NHRP servers (NHSes).

  • General: the nhrpNextIndex scalar, the NHRP Cache Table and the NHRP Purge Request Table.
  • Client: the Client Table, Client Registration Table, Client NHS Table and Client Statistics Table.
  • Server: the Server Table, Server Cache Table, Server NHC Table and Server Statistics Table.
sections.plainLanguage: The panel has three sections: one for things every device shares, one for helpers that ask for directions, and one for helpers that give them.

sections.title: The General Group: Cache and Purge Tables
sections.content:
The nhrpNextIndex scalar provides unique indices for the client index and server index in the client and server tables. Used consistently, it may prevent conflicts when several managers try to create rows in the same table at once. Reading it must give different values each time, its value must be saved in non-volatile storage if the agent is re-initialized, and it returns the special value 0 if no new rows can be created.

The NHRP Cache Table holds the internetwork-layer-to-NBMA address cache kept by both clients and servers. Its index includes an ifIndex that SHOULD reflect an interface on the NBMA subnetwork. Its indexing scheme deliberately mirrors the MPC and MPS Ingress Cache Tables in the Multiprotocol Over ATM MIB, so the two MIBs are complementary and non-overlapping.

Each cache entry records how it got there in nhrpCacheType, with eight values, and its state is incomplete, ackReply or nakReply. When an administrator creates an entry, the only type allowed is administrativelyAdded; anything else produces an inconsistentValue error. The NHRP Purge Request Table tracks purge request information.
sections.plainLanguage: The cache is a notebook of shortcuts the device has learned. Each line also notes whether someone wrote it in by hand or the device learned it by asking.

sections.title: The Client Group
sections.content:
Each row of the Client Table is a single NHC. The RequestID used in Registration requests needs to be saved to non-volatile storage. Several per-client settings come with defaults:

  • Initial request timeout: 10 seconds, in the range 1 to 900.
  • Registration, resolution and purge request retries: 3 each. A value of 0 means do not retry and 65535 means retry forever.
  • Default MTU: 9180, taken from Classical IP and ARP over ATM.
  • Hold time registered: 900 seconds.

The Client Registration Table has one entry per registration request that the client must maintain. Its state is other, registering, ackRegisterReply or nakRegisterReply. Because NHRP does not mandate a refresh algorithm, refresh information is omitted. The Client NHS Table lists the NBMA addresses of servers configured for the client, and by default the agent adds an entry for the client's default router. The Client Statistics Table holds counters for requests, replies and errors the client meets, such as resolve replies of each NAK kind, loop detected and hop count exceeded.
sections.plainLanguage: For a client you can see who it asked, whether it got an answer, and how many times it will keep asking before giving up.

sections.title: The Server Group
sections.content:
The Server Group has four tables. The Server Table has entries for each server associated with the agent. The Server Cache Table holds additional objects a server keeps for each cache entry and extends the General Group's NHRP Cache Table. The Server NHC Table has information about all the clients known to the servers. The Server Statistics Table holds counters on requests, replies and errors encountered by the servers.

Client and server rows are created by management using the read-create access, together with a RowStatus column, and the storage type of administratively added entries defaults to nonVolatile.
sections.plainLanguage: For a server you can see who it is helping, what shortcuts it remembers and how many questions it has answered.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA maintains the ADDRESS FAMILY NUMBERS name space and has placed that list in a MIB module so it can be imported into other MIBs, which means those MIBs do not need to change when a new assignment is made. This is similar to the motivation behind the IANAifType-MIB. This MIB imports AddressFamilyNumbers from that module.

The document proposes no changes to the registered numbers other than placing them into a MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared list of address kinds lives in one place, so every MIB can point to it instead of copying it.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Some objects have a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. These may be sensitive or vulnerable in some environments, and allowing SET operations without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

The MIB contains no managed objects that configure or expose NHRP security information. The RFC lists items deliberately left out because exposing them could jeopardize the entire NBMA domain: enabling or disabling security, the security parameter index (SPI), the algorithm (HMAC-MD5-128 is the default hash), the lifetime value, the key, and the list of users with access to these items. NHRP itself discusses security in Section 5.2.4.4 of RFC 2332, where an authentication option should be used to authenticate the source and protect the integrity of the NHRP payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The control panel has no knob for the secret keys. That way nobody who finds the panel can read or change them.

items.label: register
items.desc: In a server, added from a client registration.

items.label: resolveAuthoritative
items.desc: In a client, from an Authoritative NHRP Resolution Reply.

items.label: resolveNonauthoritative
items.desc: In a client, from a Nonauthoritative Resolution Reply.

items.label: transit
items.desc: In a transit server, from a forwarded NHRP packet.

items.label: administrativelyAdded
items.desc: Manually added by the administrator; the only value settable at creation.
